demographics: Risk roughly doubles every 5 years after age 65
More common in women, largely because women live longer
More common in Black and Hispanic older adults in the US, in part due to differences in vascular risk and access to care

risk_factors.text: History of traumatic brain injury, especially repeated
Fewer years of formal education or low cognitive reserve
Rare autosomal dominant mutations (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) causing early-onset disease

comorbidities: Prior stroke or transient ischemic attack
family_history: A parent or sibling with dementia or Alzheimer's disease
Rare early-onset familial cases with multiple affected relatives before age 65
social_history: Lives alone or with a spouse who has become the caregiver
Limited social engagement or recent loss of driving privileges
Retired; may have stopped hobbies and community activities

chief_complaints.text: My wife says I keep asking the same questions over and over
I keep forgetting where I put things and I can't remember appointments
I got lost driving to the grocery store I've gone to for years
My family says I'm not myself anymore

hpi.onset: Insidious, over months to a few years; family often dates it to a specific event but on careful questioning it was already present before that
hpi.duration: Usually at least 6–12 months of symptoms by the time of presentation
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive and steadily worsening; short-term memory goes first, then language, orientation, and daily function
hpi.quality: Forgetfulness of recent events and conversations while remote memories stay intact early on; repeating questions; misplacing items; trouble with words, bills, and medications
hpi.severity: Mild at first and easy to dismiss as normal aging; by presentation it is interfering with work, finances, driving, or medications
hpi.timing: Constant, worse for recent information; often more noticeable in the evening or in unfamiliar settings
aggravating: Being rushed or asked to multitask

associated_symptoms.text: Repeating the same question or story within minutes
Misplacing items, sometimes in odd places
Trouble finding words or following a conversation
Difficulty managing money, bills, or medications
Misplacing or forgetting appointments and names of acquaintances
Withdrawal from hobbies and social activities
Trouble with orientation to date or day of the week
Delusions such as believing things have been stolen
Wandering or getting up at night

pertinent_negatives: Focal weakness, numbness, or a single-sided deficit
Prominent visual hallucinations early in the course
Abrupt onset over hours to days
Fluctuating alertness from hour to hour
New incontinence early in the illness
Symptoms that began while starting a new medication

positives.text: Trouble recognizing familiar faces late in the illness
Anxiety, especially when separated from a caregiver

negatives: Visual hallucinations early in the illness
Difficulty swallowing early in the illness

positives.text: Urinary urgency or incontinence late in the illness
Slowed walking and unsteadiness late in the illness

atypical.how_it_differs: In the oldest patients, apathy, gait slowing, and withdrawal may dominate while the patient denies any memory problem; family reports the decline.
Not applicable; Alzheimer's disease does not occur in children.

general.mild: Well-groomed, alert, pleasant; may repeat questions during the visit; caregiver answers for the patient
general.moderate: Disheveled or dressed inappropriately for the weather, restless or withdrawn, needs prompting to stay on topic
general.severe: Poorly groomed, disoriented to place and time, may be agitated or apathetic, needs help with transfers
general.critical: Bedbound, mute or minimally responsive, contractures, dependent for all care

findings.finding: Cannot recall the words even with cueing

findings.maneuver: Ask the date, day of the week, month, and year

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to draw a clock showing a specific time

findings.maneuver: Listen during conversation and ask the patient to name common objects
findings.finding: Circumlocution or difficulty naming familiar items

findings.maneuver: Show a familiar object and ask the patient to identify it
findings.finding: Cannot recognize the object by sight

findings.finding: No neck stiffness or meningeal signs

labs.caveat: Hypothyroidism is a reversible cause of cognitive slowing and must be excluded; a normal TSH does not exclude Alzheimer's disease.
Low B12 is a reversible cause of memory loss and neuropathy; check even when the diet seems adequate.
Low folate can mimic or worsen cognitive impairment.
Hypercalcemia from hyperparathyroidism or malignancy can cause confusion and must be excluded.
Hyponatremia is a reversible cause of confusion; consider SIADH or diuretic effect.
Uncontrolled diabetes and hypoglycemia both worsen cognition; check fasting glucose or A1c.
Poor glycemic control is a vascular risk factor for cognitive decline.
Renal impairment affects medication dosing and can cause uremic encephalopathy.
Hepatic encephalopathy from liver disease can mimic dementia; consider if risk factors present.
Order only if hepatic encephalopathy is suspected; not routine in dementia workup.
Nonspecific; may be elevated in inflammatory or infectious causes of cognitive decline.
Nonspecific; consider if systemic inflammation or infection is suspected.
Mild elevation can occur in Alzheimer's disease; marked elevation suggests another process.
Low CSF glucose suggests infection or malignancy, not Alzheimer's disease.
Pleocytosis suggests infection or inflammation, not typical Alzheimer's disease.

findings.text: Diffuse cortical atrophy with widened sulci and ventricles
Normal-appearing brain for age (possible early in the disease)
Small vessel ischemic changes or lacunar infarcts suggesting vascular contribution

imaging.preferred_when: When MRI is unavailable or contraindicated

findings.text: Normal study (does not exclude Alzheimer's disease)
Hypometabolism in temporoparietal and posterior cingulate regions
Normal metabolic pattern (does not exclude early disease)

decision_points: Reversible causes (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, electrolyte imbalance, medication effects) must be excluded before attributing cognitive decline to Alzheimer's disease
Neuroimaging is recommended to exclude structural causes such as tumor, stroke, or hydrocephalus
Depression can mimic dementia and should be screened for and treated
Medication review for anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, and diphenhydramine is essential

criteria.name: Clinical diagnosis of probable Alzheimer's disease dementia
criteria.summary: Insidious onset over months to years, clear history of worsening cognition, and deficits in memory plus at least one other cognitive domain (language, visuospatial, executive) that interfere with daily function, with reversible causes excluded and no features suggesting another dementia.
items: Amnestic plus another cognitive domain affected
No features of another dementia (e.g., early visual hallucinations, parkinsonism before memory loss, stepwise decline)

differential.name: Delirium
differential.why_considered: Acute confusion in an older adult is often mistaken for dementia, and delirium can be superimposed on Alzheimer's disease
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset over hours to days with fluctuating alertness

history: Onset over hours to days
Fluctuating course through the day
Recent infection, surgery, new medication, or hospitalization
Inattention and easy distractibility
exam: Disoriented with waxing and waning attention
Tremor or myoclonus if withdrawal or metabolic cause
Often restless or drowsy rather than calmly forgetful
labs: Abnormal CBC, BMP, urinalysis, or TSH pointing to a medical cause
imaging: Head CT or MRI to exclude acute structural cause

differential.name: Depression with cognitive complaints (pseudodementia)
differential.why_considered: Late-life depression causes poor concentration, apathy, and memory complaints that resemble early Alzheimer's disease
differential.trigger: Prominent depressed mood, anhedonia, or recent loss with cognitive complaints

history: Sad mood, hopelessness, or loss of interest most of the day
Symptoms often date to a stressful event or bereavement
Patient emphasizes memory problems and may answer 'I don't know'
Sleep and appetite changes
exam: Depressed affect, psychomotor slowing
Cognitive effort is poor but improves with encouragement and cueing
Mini-Mental State Examination scores may vary between visits
labs: TSH and B12 to exclude reversible contributors
imaging: MRI brain usually without the medial temporal atrophy pattern of Alzheimer's disease

differential.name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
differential.why_considered: Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and cognitive slowing can be mistaken for dementia
differential.trigger: Gait apraxia and urinary incontinence early in the cognitive decline

history: Gait difficulty often precedes memory loss
Urinary urgency and incontinence early
Magnetic gait with feet seeming stuck to the floor
exam: Wide-based, shuffling gait with difficulty turning
Cognitive deficits less prominent than gait
labs: No specific blood test; diagnosis is clinical and radiologic
imaging: Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy on CT or MRI

differential.name: Vascular dementia
differential.why_considered: Second most common cause of dementia and frequently coexists with Alzheimer's disease

history: Stepwise decline with sudden drops after strokes
Focal neurologic symptoms or prior transient ischemic attack
Vascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, smoking
exam: Focal deficits, asymmetric reflexes, or gait disturbance
Executive dysfunction may be more prominent than memory loss
labs: A1c, lipids, and glucose to assess vascular risk
imaging: Multiple lacunar infarcts, white matter hyperintensities, or cortical infarcts on MRI

differential.name: Dementia with Lewy bodies
differential.why_considered: Progressive cognitive decline in an older adult with behavioral symptoms

history: Visual hallucinations early in the illness
Fluctuating alertness and attention
REM sleep behavior disorder with acting out dreams
Parkinsonism before or around the time memory loss begins
exam: Resting tremor, rigidity, or bradykinesia
Marked sensitivity to antipsychotic medications
imaging: Reduced dopamine transporter uptake on DaTscan; relative preservation of medial temporal lobes on MRI

differential.name: Frontotemporal dementia
differential.why_considered: Personality change and language difficulty in a patient with cognitive decline

history: Prominent personality change, disinhibition, or apathy early
Language difficulty with word-finding or comprehension early
Memory relatively preserved early
Younger age at onset, often 45 to 65
exam: Executive dysfunction with relatively preserved memory
Socially inappropriate behavior
imaging: Frontal and anterior temporal atrophy on MRI or hypometabolism on FDG-PET

differential.name: Medication-induced cognitive impairment
differential.why_considered: Anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, and diphenhydramine commonly cause memory and attention problems in older adults

history: Symptoms began or worsened after starting a new medication
Use of anticholinergics, sedatives, or opioids
Improvement after stopping the medication
exam: Attention and memory deficits that fluctuate with dosing
No focal neurologic findings
labs: Drug levels if applicable; otherwise normal workup
imaging: MRI brain without atrophy pattern typical of Alzheimer's disease

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Reversible cause of cognitive slowing, memory complaints, and apathy

history: Fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain
Slowly progressive cognitive slowing
exam: Dry skin, bradycardia, delayed reflexes, goiter
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4

differential.name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
differential.why_considered: Reversible cause of memory loss, neuropathy, and cognitive decline

history: Paresthesias, imbalance, or glossitis
Vegan diet, bariatric surgery, or metformin use
Macrocytic anemia
exam: Decreased vibration and proprioception
Impaired tandem gait
Hyperreflexia or extensor plantar response
labs: Low serum B12, elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine
imaging: Dorsal column changes on MRI in severe cases

severity.mild: Early stage: short-term memory lapses, repeating questions, misplacing items, and trouble with finances or medications, but the patient remains independent in basic self-care and may still drive with supervision.
severity.moderate: Middle stage: disorientation to time and place, word-finding difficulty, personality change, wandering, and needing help with dressing, bathing, and managing money; behavioral symptoms such as agitation or delusions may appear.
severity.severe: Late stage: loss of ability to communicate, recognize family, or perform any activities of daily living; incontinence, gait apraxia, swallowing difficulty, and total dependence on caregivers.
severity.critical: End stage with immobility, contractures, mutism, and inability to swallow, leading to aspiration pneumonia, pressure ulcers, and sepsis; death usually results from these complications rather than the disease itself.

red_flags.finding: Abrupt onset or stepwise decline over hours to days
red_flags.meaning: Suggests delirium, stroke, or another acute process rather than Alzheimer's disease

red_flags.finding: Focal weakness, numbness, or a new single-sided deficit
red_flags.meaning: Suggests stroke or mass lesion; needs urgent imaging
Requires evaluation for structural lesion, infection, or metabolic cause

red_flags.finding: Prominent visual hallucinations early in the illness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests dementia with Lewy bodies rather than Alzheimer's disease
Suggests Parkinson disease dementia or Lewy body dementia

red_flags.finding: Fluctuating alertness from hour to hour
red_flags.meaning: Suggests delirium or Lewy body dementia
Suggests subdural hematoma; needs urgent imaging
Suggests infection or delirium superimposed on dementia

red_flags.finding: New incontinence early in the illness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus or another structural cause

red_flags.finding: Symptoms that began while starting a new medication

complications.name: Caregiver burnout
clues: Caregiver reports exhaustion, depression, or inability to continue care

special_populations.differences: Apathy, gait slowing, and withdrawal may dominate while the patient denies memory problems; family reports the decline. Comorbidities and polypharmacy increase the risk of delirium.
Not applicable; Alzheimer's disease does not occur in children.

key_questions.question: When did the memory problems start, and how have they changed over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Insidious onset over months to years with steady worsening; abrupt onset over hours to days suggests delirium

key_questions.question: What kinds of things does he or she forget — recent conversations and appointments, or mostly names and where the keys are?
key_questions.looking_for: Forgetting recent events and conversations, repeating the same question within minutes — an amnestic pattern beyond normal aging

key_questions.question: Can he or she still manage money, bills, medications, and appointments without help?
key_questions.looking_for: Loss of independence in instrumental activities — this separates dementia from mild cognitive impairment

key_questions.question: Has he or she gotten lost in familiar places or had trouble driving?
key_questions.looking_for: Getting lost on routes driven for years; a marker of visuospatial and functional decline

key_questions.question: Is there trouble finding words, following a conversation, or reading and writing?
key_questions.looking_for: Language involvement beyond memory, supporting deficits in more than one cognitive domain

key_questions.question: Has his or her personality or mood changed — apathy, irritability, or withdrawal from hobbies?
key_questions.looking_for: Apathy, irritability, or loss of interest; common behavioral features of Alzheimer's disease

key_questions.question: Has he or she had any hallucinations, or does he or she act out dreams at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Prominent early visual hallucinations or dream enactment suggest dementia with Lewy bodies instead

key_questions.question: Has the decline been stepwise, with sudden drops after a stroke or hospitalization?
key_questions.looking_for: Stepwise decline suggests vascular contribution rather than the smooth progression of Alzheimer's disease

key_questions.question: Has there been a recent fall, head injury, or new seizure?
key_questions.looking_for: Subdural hematoma, structural lesion, or another acute cause requiring urgent imaging

key_questions.question: What medications is he or she taking, including over-the-counter sleep or allergy medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, or diphenhydramine that can cause or worsen cognitive impairment

key_questions.question: Has anyone in the family had dementia or Alzheimer's disease, especially before age 65?
key_questions.looking_for: A first-degree relative with dementia; rare early-onset familial cases with multiple affected relatives

key_questions.question: Who does he or she live with, and who helps with daily tasks?
key_questions.looking_for: Lives alone or with a spouse who has become the caregiver; caregiver stress and safety at home

key_questions.question: Does he or she smoke, drink alcohol, or use any recreational drugs?
key_questions.looking_for: Alcohol or substance use as an alternative or contributing cause of cognitive decline

key_questions.question: Has he or she had a fever, recent infection, or new illness?
key_questions.looking_for: Infection or systemic illness suggesting delirium superimposed on dementia

reasoning_points: Insidious onset over months to years with steadily progressive decline
Short-term memory impairment plus at least one other cognitive domain (language, visuospatial, or executive)
Functional decline — the patient needs help with finances, medications, driving, or appointments
Reversible causes excluded: TSH, B12, folate, electrolytes, calcium, glucose/A1c, and a medication review
Neuroimaging excludes structural causes such as tumor, stroke, subdural hematoma, or hydrocephalus
No features pointing to another dementia: no early visual hallucinations, no parkinsonism before memory loss, no stepwise decline, no early prominent gait disorder or incontinence
Collateral history from a family member is essential because the patient may underreport deficits

easy: Older adult over 65 with insidious, progressive short-term memory loss
Repeats the same question during the visit
Family reports getting lost in familiar places
Normal focal neurologic exam with no tremor or weakness
medium: Patient denies any problem and the family provides the whole history
Prominent apathy or depression that raises the question of pseudodementia
Coexisting vascular risk factors and white matter changes on MRI
Mild cognitive impairment at the borderline of dementia
Medication list includes an anticholinergic that must be sorted out
hard: Early-onset disease before age 65 with a strong family history
Atypical presentation with language or visuospatial deficits dominating over memory
Delirium superimposed on dementia after a hospitalization
Oldest-old patient with gait slowing and withdrawal but no self-reported memory complaint
Diagnostic uncertainty requiring FDG-PET or amyloid PET to distinguish from frontotemporal or Lewy body dementia
